messages.subject: The function choose.files() on OSs other than Windoze
messages.subject_clean: The function choose.files() on OSs other than Windoze
messages.body_plain:
Hi all

If you have used R on Windoze but don't usually do so, you will know
that the very convenient function choose.files only works on Windoze.
While you can of course run R for Windows on Linux (with Wine) or use

tk_choose.files() # from library(tcltk)

I still missed the possibility to not just  move around directories
easily and choose more than one file (which tk_choose.files() offers),
but also create a file or even a directory and then also immediately
make that the working directory. For some time I had scribbled
together a function choose.path that did pretty much that, but I
didn't really like how I did that there. I now wrote an at least
slightly better function choose.files that does not rely on other
packages and that I use on Linux. While I have done a bit of testing
myself and didn't immediately run into problems, I'd appreciate any
feedback on it that you might have, e.g., if you find something
doesn't work or if you think a feature is missing (and, you don't have
to write me to only say it's not elegant, I know that myself ;-)). I
put the function on my website for now so if you enter this into R:

source("http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/
choose.files.r")

then you can use the function much like you can do in Windoze (it
doesn't have the default=... but some other arguments you can play
around with). Like I said, any feedback would be much appreciated and,
if it leads to me changing the code, of course acknowledged.

Cheers,
STG

messages.subject: Testing independence of frequency of VP ellipsis between interlocutors
messages.subject_clean: Testing independence of frequency of VP ellipsis between interlocutors
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I realize this is a very basic question, but I have been doing quite a
bit of reading and am still uncertain how best to proceed here. I do
have this book, so if I have overlooked something useful therein,
please feel free to refer me back to it.  :)

My data consists of counts of a VP ellipsis used in conversations
between pairs of interlocutors (from the Switchboard corpus). The
hypothesis I want to test is the following: more frequent use of this
VP ellipsis by one speaker will tend to increase the frequency of the
VP ellipsis by the other speaker (i.e., this might be evidence of a
priming effect).

So I just have two vectors, the counts for speaker A and the counts
for speaker B are the columns, and if they are lined up each row
represents a particular conversation, like this:

A B
0 1
0 2
1 0
3 1
0 2
2 0
2 1

There are about 420 conversations (rows). There are lots of zeros in
this data. So the first row {0,1} means that in the first
conversation, speaker A used no VP ellipsis and speaker B used it
once.

What would be the best way to analyze this data?

messages.subject_clean: default charset encoding for R output?
messages.body_plain:
It looks like the encoding for the output in R is OS-dependent.
I tested on Win, Ubuntu, and Mac.

I asked R to read in utf8 files and then output it without any re-
encoding. It turned out that the encoding for Win output is big5 while
those in Ubuntu and Mac are UTF8.

In short, everything works well as long as it's not in windoze.....

Alvin Chen

>
> In Windows XP, when I asked R to read in big5 files, then processed
> the data and saved the dataframe in a csv file, the encoding of the
> csv is Windows Chinese Traditional Big5 (I got this encoding from
> OpenOffice).
>
> But in Mac, when I asked R to read in UTF16-BE files, then processed
> the data and saved the dataframe in a csv file, the encoding of the
> csv is UTF-8.
>
> I didn't do any re-encoding in the R script. So I'm wondering if
> there's any default charset encoding for R outputs?
>
> Thanks in advance.
>
> Best,
>
> Alvin Chen

messages.subject: Backref argument in strapply
messages.body_plain:
Hello, Rists. I have a question about the backref argument of
strapply.

I was working on the "Other applications 5: web crawling / compiling a
web-based corpus" assignment and kept getting this error message:

trying URL 'http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/teaching/
qclwr/web/<a HREF="02.html"'
Error in download.file(current.pages[j], paste(counter, "___",
basename(current.pages[j]),  :
  cannot open URL 'http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries/
teaching/qclwr/web/<a HREF="02.html"'

I narrowed the problem down to this line of code in Stefan's solution:

         current.links.1<-unlist(strapply(website, "<a[^<]*?href=\"(?!
#)(?!mailto)(.*?(html?|txt))\"", ignore.case=T, perl=T, backref=-1))

Even though the backref was set to "-1", and therefore only supposed
to return the back-referenced part "(.*?(html?|txt))", it returned the
whole match, beginning with the "<a", as you can see in the URL in the
error message. Out of curiosity I changed the backref argument to "1"
and the script finally worked without problems. If I'm reading
correctly the documentation for strapply ("If negative then only the
that number of backreferences are passed but the match itself is
not.") the backref argument "-1" should have given me the correct
links. Am I reading something wrong? I assume strapply doesn't work
differently on a Mac, right? I fixed the problem, so this post is more
for my understanding of strapply. (I, too, am looking forward to
strapplyc, by the way.)

Thanks for all your collective R wisdom. Earl Brown

Hm, yes, as you wrote

"Even though the backref was set to "-1", and therefore only supposed
to return the back-referenced part "(.*?(html?|txt))", it returned the

whole match [...]" I am getting the same problem here, and backref=1
does the job.

Off the top of my head, that is kinda confusing so I tried this:

#########################
rm(list=ls(all=TRUE))
library(gsubfn)
qwe <- c("abcdef", "ghijkl", "mbcdef")

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If zero or positive the match is passed as the first argument to the
replacement function followed by the indicated number of
backreferences as subsequent arguments.
strapply(qwe, "(.)b", perl=TRUE, backref=1)
[[1]]
[1] "a"

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "m"

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If negative then only the that number of backreferences are passed

but the match itself is not.

strapply(qwe, "(.)b", perl=TRUE, backref=-1)
[[1]]
[1] "ab"

[[2]]
NULL

[[3]]
[1] "mb"
#########################

The output doesn't seem to be what one would expect. And here is a
maybe more confusing example from strapply's help page:

#########################
# running window of 5 characters using 0-lookahead perl regexp
# Note that the three ( in the regexp will fool it into thinking there
# are three backreferences so specify backref explicitly.
x <- "abcdefghijkl"

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If negative then only the that number of backreferences are passed

but the match itself is not.

# THIS! is the code Gabor provides, but probably not the result he intended?
strapply(x, "(.)(?=(....))",  paste0, backref = -2, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
[1] "aabcde" "bbcdef" "ccdefg" "ddefgh" "eefghi" "ffghij" "gghijk" "hhijkl"

# the following comment is quoted from the help page of gsubfn, to
which the help page of strapply refers the reader
# If zero or positive the match is passed as the first argument to the
replacement function followed by the indicated number of
backreferences as subsequent arguments.
# THIS! is not the code Gabor provides, but probably the result he intended?
strapply(x, "(.)(?=(....))",  paste0, backref = 2, perl = TRUE)[[1]]
[1] "abcde" "bcdef" "cdefg" "defgh" "efghi" "fghij" "ghijk" "hijkl"
#########################

Weird ...

Re the assignment script: One can of course use this:

sub("^.*?\"", "",
exact.matches("<a[^<]*?href=\"(?!#)(?!mailto).*?(html?|txt)(?=\")",
website, case.sens=FALSE)[[1]], perl=TRUE)

Still, the strapply approach is nicer but right now - it's late here -
I don't see the logic esp. in the example from the website itself ...

STG
--

messages.subject: Re: Backref argument in strapply
messages.body_plain:
Apparently, the tcl engine and the R engine treat the backref argument
differently, as switching the perl argument seems to switch the
polarity of the backref argument. Gabor says in this post
http://groups.google.com/group/corpling-with-r/browse_thread/thread/d30502e17afee11f
that: "Using perl = TRUE will cause strapply to use the slower R
engine whereas by default strapply uses faster tcl engine (if you
don't specify perl and if you have tcltk installed)."

Thus, I get the one result, the same result, if I use

perl=FALSE, backref=-1
or
perl=TRUE, backref=1

and a different result if I use

perl=TRUE, backref=-1
or
perl=FALSE, backref=1

Here's a simple example to illustrate:

> text<-"Some sentence whatever it may be."

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=FALSE, backref=-1))
[1] "whatever"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=TRUE, backref=1))
[1] "whatever"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=TRUE, backref=-1))
[1] "sentence whatever it"

> unlist(strapply(text, "sentence (whatever) it", perl=FALSE, backref=1))
[1] "sentence whatever it"

I don't know what engines are (tcl versus R engine) but it appears
that the problem might have to do with the engine that strapply uses.

Thanks for the exact.matches()[[1]] plus gsub() work-around. Earl Brown

Thanks for finding and investigating this.   Its supposed to process
the match plus the back references if backref >= 0 and only the back
references otherwise.  Thus the "tcl" engine seems to be working as
expected but the "R" engine has it backwards.  I have just committed a
fix to the development version so the corrected version can be fetched
from there like this:

> library(gsubfn)
Loading required package: proto
> source("http://gsubfn.googlecode.com/svn-history/r81/trunk/R/gsubfn.R")
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = -1, engine = "R")
[1] "b/c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = 1, engine = "R")
[1] "ab b/ac c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = -1)
Loading required package: tcltk
Loading Tcl/Tk interface ... done
[1] "b/c"
> gsubfn("a(.)", paste, "ab/ac", backref = 1)
[1] "ab b/ac c"

messages.subject: RE: [CorpLing with R] error in tolower
messages.body_plain:
Your problem is that \xa1\xaf is not a valid utf8 sequence.  If it resulted from "save as text" then whoever did it must have saved it to a non-Unicdoe encoding. I thought it might be big5, but the Big5 for curvy-apostrophe is \xa1\xa6 (close but not quite the same). Without knowing what encoding it actually is (and therefore what to tell iconv to change it from) you probably have no option except to work out a list of global search and replaces for each of the dodgy sequences.

best

Andrew.
